items.readable_text:
Content:
When attempting to construct a mathematical proof, it's often a good idea to start with some specific cases. Proving results for particular cases usually gives valuable insights into how to construct the proof of a more general result.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll prove specific cases of the addition, scalar multiplication, and division properties of modular arithmetic.

Content:
We start with our definition of modular congruence:

Content:
> Let [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] be integers and let [MATH: n] be a positive integer. We say that [MATH: \boldsymbol a] is congruent to [MATH: \boldsymbol b] modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol n] if and only if [MATH: n\mid (a-b).] If [MATH: a] is congruent to [MATH: b] modulo [MATH: n,] we write
> [MATH: a\equiv b\quad (\textrm{mod }n).]

Content:
Since the definition of congruence uses the concept of divisibility, let's also state this definition:

Content:
> Let [MATH: c] and [MATH: d] be integers with [MATH: d\neq 0]. We say that [MATH: \boldsymbol d] divides [MATH: \boldsymbol c] if there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that [MATH: c=d\cdot k.]

Content:
Putting these two definitions together, we have the following chain of equivalences:

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n)
\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
n \mid (a-b)
\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
a-b = nk]
for some integer [MATH: k.]

Content:
Let's construct a direct proof of the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{a \equiv b}_{P(a,b)} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{a+2 \equiv b+2}_{Q(a,b)} \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 5)]

Content:
We start by assuming the antecedent [MATH: P] is true.

Content:
> Assume that [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 5).]

Content:
Next, we state what this means using the definition of congruence.

Content:
> By the definition of modular congruence,
> [MATH: 5 \mid (a-b)
> \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
> a-b = 5k]
> for some integer [MATH: k.]

Content:
Now, the goal is to show that

Content:
[MATH: (a+2) \equiv (b+2) \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad 5 \mid \big( (a+2) - (b+2)\big).]

Content:
So, we write down the difference between [MATH: (a+2)] and [MATH: (b+2)] and show that it is a multiple of [MATH: 5] using our assumption regarding the difference between [MATH: a] and [MATH: b{:}]

Content:
> Hence, we get
> [MATH: (a + 2) − (b + 2)|= a + 2 − b − 2; = a − b; = 5k.]

Content:
Since [MATH: (a+2) - (b+2)] is a multiple of [MATH: 5,] this shows that [MATH: (a+2) \equiv (b+2)] modulo [MATH: 5.] So, our proof is complete, and we write our conclusion.

Content:
> Therefore, according to the definition of congruence, we have
> [MATH: a+2 \equiv b+2 \quad (\textrm{mod} \: 5).]

Content:
Now that we've discussed all the details, let's write down our final proof.

Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence in reverse:

According to the definition of modular congruence, the final equation implies that [MATH: 8a \equiv 8b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 10).]

Content:
Recall the following division properties of modular arithmetic for [MATH: k\neq 0{:}]

Content:
- The first division property states that
[MATH: ka \equiv kb \quad(\text{mod}\,kn) \quad \Rightarrow \quad a \equiv b \quad(\textrm{mod}\,n).]

Content:
- The second division property states that
[MATH: \left(ka\equiv kb\:(\textrm{mod} \,n)\right) \:\land\: \left(\textrm{gcd}(k,n)=1\right) \quad \Rightarrow\quad a \equiv b \quad(\textrm{mod}\, n).]

Content:
Let's prove that the second property holds in the following case:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{3a \equiv 3b}_{P(a,b)} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{a \equiv b}_{Q(a,b)} \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 4)]

Content:
We begin our proof by assuming [MATH: P] is true.

Content:
> Assume [MATH: 3a \equiv 3b\:(\textrm{mod} \: 4).]
>
> Then, by the definition of modular congruence, we have
> [MATH: 3a≡3b(mod4)|⇔4∣(3a − 3b); ⇔4∣3(a − b).]

Content:
Now, we recall the following divisibility property of integers:
[MATH: (c \mid ab) \:\land\: (\textrm{gcd}(a,c)=1) \quad\Rightarrow\quad (c \mid b)]
Using this fact, we have the following:

Content:
> Now, since [MATH: 3(a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: 4] and [MATH: \textrm{gcd}(4,3)=1,] the difference [MATH: (a-b)] must be divisible by [MATH: 4,] i.e.,
> [MATH: 4 \mid (a-b).]

Content:
Finally, we use the definition of modular congruence one more:

Content:
> Therefore, according to the definition of modular congruence, we have
> [MATH: a \equiv b \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 4).]

Content:
And we're done.

Content:
Let's restate the full proof.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When attempting to construct a mathematical proof, it's often a good idea to start with some specific cases. Proving results for particular cases usually gives valuable insights into how to construct the proof of a more general result.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll prove specific cases of the addition, scalar multiplication, and division properties of modular arithmetic.

Content:
We start with our definition of modular congruence:

Content:
> Let [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] be integers and let [MATH: n] be a positive integer. We say that [MATH: \boldsymbol a] is congruent to [MATH: \boldsymbol b] modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol n] if and only if [MATH: n\mid (a-b).] If [MATH: a] is congruent to [MATH: b] modulo [MATH: n,] we write
> [MATH: a\equiv b\quad (\textrm{mod }n).]

Content:
Since the definition of congruence uses the concept of divisibility, let's also state this definition:

Content:
> Let [MATH: c] and [MATH: d] be integers with [MATH: d\neq 0]. We say that [MATH: \boldsymbol d] divides [MATH: \boldsymbol c] if there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that [MATH: c=d\cdot k.]

Content:
Putting these two definitions together, we have the following chain of equivalences:

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: n)
\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
n \mid (a-b)
\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
a-b = nk]
for some integer [MATH: k.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Proving a Congruence Statement

Content:
Let's construct a direct proof of the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{a \equiv b}_{P(a,b)} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \underbrace{a+2 \equiv b+2}_{Q(a,b)} \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 5)]

Content:
We start by assuming the antecedent [MATH: P] is true.

Content:
> Assume that [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 5).]

Content:
Next, we state what this means using the definition of congruence.

Content:
> By the definition of modular congruence,
> [MATH: 5 \mid (a-b)
> \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
> a-b = 5k]
> for some integer [MATH: k.]

Content:
Now, the goal is to show that

Content:
[MATH: (a+2) \equiv (b+2) \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad 5 \mid \big( (a+2) - (b+2)\big).]

Content:
So, we write down the difference between [MATH: (a+2)] and [MATH: (b+2)] and show that it is a multiple of [MATH: 5] using our assumption regarding the difference between [MATH: a] and [MATH: b{:}]

Content:
> Hence, we get
> [MATH: (a + 2) − (b + 2)|= a + 2 − b − 2; = a − b; = 5k.]

Content:
Since [MATH: (a+2) - (b+2)] is a multiple of [MATH: 5,] this shows that [MATH: (a+2) \equiv (b+2)] modulo [MATH: 5.] So, our proof is complete, and we write our conclusion.

Content:
> Therefore, according to the definition of congruence, we have
> [MATH: a+2 \equiv b+2 \quad (\textrm{mod} \: 5).]

Content:
Now that we've discussed all the details, let's write down our final proof.

---

Content:
Proposition:

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad\Rightarrow\quad a+2 \equiv b+2 \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 5)]

Content:
Proof:

Content:
> Assume that [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod} \: 5).] By the definition of modular congruence,
> [MATH: 5 \mid (a-b)
> \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
> a-b = 5k]
> for some integer [MATH: k.] Hence, we get
> [MATH: (a + 2) − (b + 2)|= a + 2 − b − 2; = a − b; = 5k.]
> Therefore, according to the definition of congruence, we have
> [MATH: a+2 \equiv b+2 \qquad (\textrm{mod} \: 5).]
